newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Pepper a hot commodity in S.E.Asia as prices soar.
newsitem.headline: Pepper a hot commodity in S.E.Asia as prices soar.

text.p: Southeast Asian producers are racing to cash in on soaring pepper prices, spurred by strong demand from abroad and a squeeze on supplies worldwide which has drawn speculators into this overheated commodity market.
In Vietnam, black pepper growers are grinding out exports from what looks set to be a bumper harvest, but in Indonesia production has slumped after heavy rainfall hit the crop.
"They are exporting really rapidly now because prices are good," one trader in Vietnam said on Monday. He said prices had climbed to $3,000 a tonne FOB Saigon Port from $2,500 in early January.
There is a global shortage of both black and white pepper, exacerbated by growing demand from the major market in the United States.

"Chinese and Sri Lankan grades are not easily available. Indonesia is having problems with its supplies. Mexican grades are also in short supply and so the demand is high for the Malabar pepper from India," Indian exporter G.A.Balakrishnan told Reuters.
India produces about a third of the world's pepper output of 180,000 tonnes. The other major producers include Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam.
Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Pepper Exporters, said the country's black pepper production was expected to fall to 14,000 tonnes in 1997 from 16,000 tonnes last year.
"Production is expected to decline as a result of heavy rainfall which affected the fruiting process," he said.
Indonesian traders said black pepper export prices were quoted at around $3,500-$3,600 a tonne, compared with an average $2,500 last year and $1,800 in 1995.
"Prices are increasing but the problem is we do not have much to sell. That is what has been driving up prices," said one. He said the main crop harvest peaks between May and June.
"Harvesting has begun but the quantities are very limited at the moment."
The trader said Indonesian carry-over stocks had almost run out as exporters have been selling them over the past two years in the face of the decline in production.
Quoting data obtained from a leading European trading house, the trader said global black exports fluctuated at between 100,000 and 120,000 tonnes a year.

He said Indonesia's exports were forecast to reach 12,000 tonnes in 1996/97 (July/June), India's exports 25,000 tonnes and Brazil 9,000 tonnes. This compared with 30,000 tonnes for Indonesia in 1995/96, 35,000 tonnes for India and 14,500 tonnes for Brazil.
Indonesia's black pepper is grown mainly in the Lampung region of South Sumatra and some 90 percent of exports go to the United States.
Vietnam's pepper output is normally between 15,000 and 20,000 tonnes a year and is expected to be at the top of that range in 1997.
Domestic consumption accounts for more than 2,000 tonnes.
Traders estimated that over 14,000 tonnes had been exported so far this year and sales from the annual harvest usually continue until August.

However, traders said they expected a final 3,000 tonnes to be sold in coming weeks, partly because this year's harvest started a month earlier than normal -- at the end of January -- and because sellers have been cashing in on the rise in prices.

Some 60 percent of Vietnam's exports go through Singapore before being shipped on to the Middle East, Europe, Africa and Pakistan. Reliable figures for exports to China are not available, though traders put sales to China so far this year at 3,000 tonnes.

Traders said that Vietnam's black pepper market was still unsophisticated. Exporters rarely keep abreast of developments in the world market and quality suffers because they cannot afford processing equipment.

"The problem for Vietnam's pepper is that exporters are not very well informed," one Western trader said. "Although they do have access to some information, in my opinion they don't really use it. If they did, they would probably make better profits."

About 60 percent of the country's output comes from the southern province of Song Be, while most of the rest is grown in the neighbouring provinces of Dak Lak and Dong Nai and on the island of Phu Quoc in the Gulf of Thailand.
